items.stem: Rahul visits a science laboratory where a researcher is looking at plant cells. The researcher explains that human eyes have a limit of resolution of 0.1 mm, meaning we cannot see things smaller than that clearly. She shows Rahul a light microscope and explains that the eyepiece has a 10X magnification power and the objective lens is set to 40X. Rahul looks through it and sees tiny box-like structures. He then spots a poster showing highly detailed, nanoscale structures of a cell. The researcher says that image was taken using a different, far more powerful instrument that uses beams of electrons instead of light. QUESTIONS: (a) Calculate the total magnification of the light microscope Rahul looked through. (b) Why is a microscope an essential tool for studying cells? (c) Name the more powerful instrument used to take the picture of the nanoscale details on the poster. (d) What is meant by the limit of resolution of the human eye?
items.answer: (a) The total magnification of the light microscope is 400X. This is calculated by multiplying the magnification of the eyepiece (10X) by the magnification of the objective lens (40X). (b) A microscope is essential because most cells are much smaller than 0.1 mm, which is the limit of resolution of the unaided human eye. The microscope magnifies the image, allowing us to see these tiny structures clearly. (c) The more powerful instrument is the electron microscope. It uses a beam of electrons to reveal fine details at the nanometre scale. (d) The limit of resolution is the point at which two close objects can no longer be seen as separate distinct points by the human eye. For a normal human eye at 25 cm, this limit is about 0.1 mm.

items.stem: Meera is preparing a fresh salad for dinner. She cuts cucumbers and tomatoes into a bowl and sprinkles a generous amount of salt over them. She leaves the bowl on the kitchen counter and goes to read a book. After an hour, she returns and notices that a lot of watery liquid has collected at the bottom of the bowl, and the cucumber pieces have become soft and shrunk in size. Her mother explains that this happens due to a natural process where water moves across the selectively permeable boundaries of the vegetable cells due to the salt added on the outside. QUESTIONS: (a) Name the scientific process responsible for the release of water from the cucumber cells. (b) What type of solution did the sprinkled salt create around the cucumber cells? (c) How does the cell membrane act during this process? (d) What would have happened to the cucumber pieces if Meera had placed them in a bowl of pure water instead of adding salt?
items.answer: (a) The process responsible for the release of water is osmosis. (b) The sprinkled salt created a hypertonic solution outside the cells. This means the solute concentration outside was higher than the inside of the cells, causing water to move out. (c) The cell membrane acts as a selectively permeable membrane. It allows water molecules to pass through it while blocking other larger or dissolved substances. (d) If placed in pure water, the surrounding medium would be a hypotonic solution. Water would move into the cucumber cells by osmosis, causing them to swell and become firm.

items.stem: During a severe monsoon storm, high speed winds and heavy rainfall batter the trees in a local neighbourhood. Despite the immense pressure and stress from the harsh environment, the large trees stand tall, and their green leaves retain their shape without bursting from the excess rainwater. The next day in school, the science teacher uses this real-life event to explain how plant cells differ from animal cells. She mentions that while plants lack a bony skeleton, their cells have a special rigid outer covering. This layer provides structural support and helps them withstand tough environmental conditions and changes in moisture. QUESTIONS: (a) Identify the special rigid outer covering present in plant cells that the teacher is referring to. (b) Name the chemical substance that primarily makes up this outer layer in plants. (c) If animal cells were placed in a highly dilute external environment like rainwater, they might swell and burst. Why do plant cells not burst under the same conditions?
items.answer: (a) The special rigid outer covering is the cell wall. (b) The plant cell wall is primarily made up of cellulose, which is a complex carbohydrate that provides structural strength. (c) Plant cells do not burst because the rigid cell wall exerts an opposing pressure against the swelling cell interior. This allows plant cells to withstand highly dilute (hypotonic) external media without bursting, unlike animal cells which lack this rigid wall.

items.stem: A microbiologist is examining a water sample from a hot spring under an electron microscope. She observes single-celled organisms that lack a well-defined nucleus. Their genetic material is simply present as a single circular molecule lying in a specific region of the cytoplasm. Later, she compares this with a sample of human cheek cells, which are much larger. The human cells have a distinct, large spherical structure in the center covered by a double-layered nuclear membrane, which safely houses thread-like structures containing the genetic information required for inheritance. QUESTIONS: (a) What term is used to describe the undefined nuclear region in the single-celled organisms from the hot spring? (b) Based on the cell structure, classify the two types of organisms observed by the microbiologist. (c) What are the thread-like structures found in the human cheek cells called, and what is their main chemical component? (d) State one structural difference between the two types of cells mentioned in the passage, other than the nuclear region.
items.answer: (a) The undefined nuclear region containing the genetic material in these simple organisms is called the nucleoid. (b) The single-celled organisms from the hot spring are prokaryotic cells, while the human cheek cells are eukaryotic cells. (c) The thread-like structures are called chromatin material or chromosomes. They are primarily composed of DNA (Deoxyribonucleic acid) and specific proteins. (d) Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles, whereas eukaryotic cells have several membrane-bound organelles like mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum.

items.stem: In a biology class, a teacher compares a eukaryotic cell to a busy manufacturing factory. She explains that one part of the cell acts as a manufacturing unit consisting of a network of tubes where proteins and lipids are synthesized. Once produced, these materials are sent to a packaging center comprising stacks of flattened sacs. Here, they are modified, sorted, and packed into small vesicles. Finally, the teacher mentions a specialized waste disposal system in the factory. This system consists of tiny membrane-bound sacs filled with powerful enzymes that break down any damaged machinery or foreign waste, keeping the cell clean. QUESTIONS: (a) Identify the manufacturing unit of the cell responsible for synthesizing lipids. (b) Which cell organelle acts as the packaging center mentioned in the passage? (c) Name the waste disposal system of the cell. (d) Why is the rough endoplasmic reticulum considered rough, and what is its specific function? (e) What might happen to the cell if the waste disposal sacs accidentally burst open?
items.answer: (a) The Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum (SER) is responsible for the synthesis of lipids and fats. (b) The Golgi apparatus acts as the packaging and shipping center of the cell. (c) The lysosomes act as the waste disposal and clean-up system of the cell. (d) The rough endoplasmic reticulum looks rough under a microscope because it has tiny particles called ribosomes attached to its surface. Its specific function is protein synthesis. (e) If lysosomes burst open, their powerful digestive enzymes would be released into the cytoplasm and digest the cell’s own organelles, ultimately leading to the destruction of the cell.

items.stem: Rohan is a marathon runner who trains for several hours every day. His coach emphasizes the importance of a proper diet to keep his stamina high. During a sports science seminar, a doctor explains that endurance athletes need highly efficient muscle cells. These muscle cells contain a large number of specific double-membrane organelles that break down glucose from food to release massive amounts of energy for cellular activities. The doctor notes that the inner membrane of this organelle is deeply folded to maximize the surface area for energy-producing chemical reactions. QUESTIONS: (a) Name the cell organelle being discussed by the doctor. (b) What is the biological name for the deep folds of the inner membrane, and why is this folding important? (c) In what chemical form is the energy released and stored by this organelle?
items.answer: (a) The organelle being discussed is the mitochondrion, often called the powerhouse of the cell. (b) The deep folds of the inner membrane are called cristae. This folding is important because it vastly increases the surface area available for the chemical reactions that generate energy. (c) The energy is released and stored in the form of ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate) molecules, which act as the energy currency of the cell.

items.stem: An agricultural scientist is studying a farm where potatoes and tomatoes are grown. She observes the bright red colour of the ripe tomatoes, which easily attracts birds and insects. She then digs up some potatoes, noting they are thick, colourless underground stems packed with starch to provide nutrition for the plant. Back in the laboratory, she explains to her intern that both the red pigments in the tomatoes and the starch storage in the potatoes are managed by the exact same category of specialized organelles, which are found exclusively in plant cells. QUESTIONS: (a) What is the general term for the category of specialized organelles mentioned by the scientist? (b) Which specific type of this organelle is responsible for the bright red and orange colours of fruits like tomatoes? (c) Name the specific colourless organelle that stores starch in the potatoes. (d) Explain the primary function of chloroplasts, another organelle belonging to this same category.
items.answer: (a) The general term for these specialized organelles is plastids. (b) Chromoplasts are the plastids responsible for the bright colours (other than green) in flowers and fruits. (c) Leucoplasts are the colourless plastids responsible for storing food materials such as starch, oils, or proteins. (d) Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll and are responsible for synthesizing food for the plant by absorbing sunlight during the process of photosynthesis.

items.stem: Sunita goes on a family vacation for a week and forgets to ask her neighbour to water her potted indoor plants. When she returns, she finds that the plants look severely wilted, with their leaves drooping lifelessly downwards. She immediately waters them thoroughly. By the next morning, she is amazed to see that the leaves are standing firm and upright again. Her elder brother, a biology student, explains that mature plant cells have large central storage sacs filled with a fluid. The pressure from this fluid pushes against the cell boundaries, helping maintain the shape and firmness of the plant. QUESTIONS: (a) Identify the large central storage sacs in plant cells described by Sunita’s brother. (b) What is the watery fluid contained inside these storage sacs called? (c) Explain scientifically why the plant leaves drooped when they lacked water and became firm again after watering.
items.answer: (a) The large central storage sacs in plant cells are called vacuoles. (b) The watery fluid inside the plant vacuole is called cell sap. (c) When the plant lacked water, the vacuoles lost their stored water, reducing internal pressure and causing the cells to become less firm, leading to wilting. Upon watering, the vacuoles absorbed water and swelled, restoring pressure against the cell wall and keeping the plant firm and upright.

items.stem: A young boy, Aryan, scrapes his knee badly while playing football. A thick scab forms, and after a few days, the skin completely heals as new skin cells replace the damaged ones. Around the same time, Aryan’s mother gives birth to a baby girl. Aryan’s grandmother comments that the new baby has eyes exactly like her father but hair like her mother. Aryan wonders how his skin can perfectly copy itself to heal his wound, while his new baby sister looks like a complex mixture of traits from both parents. QUESTIONS: (a) Which type of cell division is responsible for healing Aryan’s scraped knee by replacing damaged cells? (b) How does the number of chromosomes in the newly formed skin cells compare to the original skin cells? (c) Name the type of cell division that produces the gametes in the parents, ultimately leading to the birth of the baby sister. (d) Why does the second type of cell division result in the baby sharing traits from both parents rather than being an identical copy?
items.answer: (a) Mitosis is the type of cell division responsible for growth, repair, and healing of damaged tissues like Aryan’s scraped knee. (b) In mitosis, the new daughter cells have exactly the same number of chromosomes as the original parent cell. They are genetically identical. (c) Meiosis is the type of cell division that occurs in reproductive organs to produce gametes (sperm and eggs). (d) Meiosis involves two divisions that halve the chromosome number. When a sperm and egg fuse during fertilization, the baby receives half of its genetic information from the mother and half from the father, creating genetic diversity rather than an identical copy.

items.stem: Mr. Sharma recently visited a doctor for a routine check-up and discovered a small, unusual lump on his arm. The doctor performed a biopsy and explained the results using basic biological principles. He told Mr. Sharma that normal cells in the human body grow, divide, and eventually die in a highly regulated manner. They naturally stop dividing when they come into contact with neighbouring cells. However, in Mr. Sharma’s lump, a few cells had lost this vital control mechanism. They ignored signals to stop growing and continued dividing uncontrollably. QUESTIONS: (a) What is the medical term for the mass of abnormal cells that formed the lump on Mr. Sharma’s arm? (b) Name the natural phenomenon where normal cells stop dividing upon coming into contact with neighbouring cells. (c) According to the classical Cell Theory, where do all the new cells in Mr. Sharma’s body originate from? (d) What is Programmed Cell Death (PCD) and why is it essential for the body? (e) Name the three scientists whose work collectively led to the formulation of the Cell Theory.
items.answer: (a) The mass of abnormal cells resulting from uncontrolled division is called a tumour. (b) The phenomenon is called contact inhibition. Normal cells show this property to prevent uncontrolled growth. (c) According to the Cell Theory, all new cells arise from pre-existing cells through the process of cell division. (d) Programmed Cell Death (PCD) is a genetically regulated process of selective cell destruction. It is essential for normal development, cellular quality control, maintaining balance, and immune function. (e) The scientists are Matthias Schleiden, Theodor Schwann, and Rudolf Virchow.
